answer.answer:
Teriflunomide, approved for multiple sclerosis, drives uridine-reversible myeloid differentiation of cytarabine-residual oxidative AML cells by DHODH inhibition

Hypothesis. Teriflunomide, originally approved for relapsing multiple sclerosis (unverified prior knowledge; this packet has no product label), is predicted to inhibit dihydroorotate dehydrogenase (DHODH) at verified clinical exposures and to induce myeloid differentiation in cytarabine-residual acute myeloid leukemia cells that rely on oxidative metabolism. The primary endpoint is differentiation with reduced disease-initiating capacity, larger in that residual population than in normal CD34-positive hematopoietic stem and progenitor cells. Venetoclax plus azacitidine is an established AML regimen and is used only as a mechanistic comparator [S3].

Supported premises. In specimens studied by Lagadinou and colleagues, functionally defined leukemia stem cells frequently had low reactive oxygen species and elevated BCL-2, and BCL-2 inhibition reduced oxidative phosphorylation and affected quiescent leukemia stem cells [S1]. The finding supports study of discrete metabolic dependencies and of selectivity; a therapeutic window for other mitochondrial inhibitors remains unshown [S1]. In cytarabine-treated models, Farge and colleagues found residual cells that were not consistently enriched for immature quiescent leukemia stem cells, that carried mitochondrial and fatty-acid-oxidation-related oxidative metabolism, and whose altered metabolic state changed treatment response [S2]. That residual population is therefore a separate biological context from the ROS-low stem-cell fraction [S1], and the work does not establish clinical efficacy of a new compound [S2]. Sykes and colleagues showed that DHODH inhibition promoted myeloid differentiation and affected disease-related endpoints in experimental AML models, connecting this metabolic step to differentiation [S4]. Whether any approved drug that affects the pathway matches that exposure and selectivity remains open [S4]. Pollyea and colleagues linked venetoclax–azacitidine to changes in leukemia-stem-cell TCA-cycle and oxidative-phosphorylation metabolism in patient-associated material and follow-up experiments [S3].

Speculative bridges. Unverified prior knowledge holds that teriflunomide, the active metabolite of leflunomide, inhibits DHODH. The packet does not name the inhibitor in [S4], so a shared target is an assumption. A second assumption is that unbound concentrations from approved multiple-sclerosis dosing engage AML DHODH comparably to the experimental blockade tied to differentiation [S4]. Unverified prior knowledge places DHODH on the inner mitochondrial membrane, where it reduces ubiquinone. It is speculated that cytarabine-residual cells with high oxidative demand [S2] translate partial DHODH blockade into differentiation [S4], while quiescent ROS-low leukemia stem cells [S1] have lower pyrimidine flux and respond less. The packet contains no teriflunomide, DHODH, or pyrimidine measurements in AML.

Alternative explanations. Observed activity could be bulk cytostasis from nucleotide depletion without maturation; killing limited to the ROS-low BCL-2-high fraction [S1]; an off-target effect; venetoclax-like oxidative-phosphorylation collapse without differentiation [S3]; or matched toxicity in normal progenitors, which would erase a therapeutic margin.

Discriminating preclinical test. From each primary AML sample, separate a ROS-low fraction, the complementary bulk, and cells persisting after brief ex vivo cytarabine, with healthy-donor CD34-positive cells as the normal comparator. Apply teriflunomide at concentrations anchored, after pharmacokinetic verification, to total and unbound levels used in multiple sclerosis, plus one higher concentration solely to confirm biochemical suppression. Calibrate with a non-approved tool DHODH inhibitor, and include venetoclax for oxidative-phosphorylation and stem-cell comparison [S3]. Read, as separate endpoints, dihydroorotate and UTP (target engagement), myeloid markers, morphology, and colony maturity (differentiation [S4]), viability (killing), oxygen consumption (oxidative metabolism [S1][S2]), and limiting-dilution engraftment. Repeat informative doses with exogenous uridine. Unverified prior knowledge expects uridine repletion to reverse on-target DHODH effects; rescue is therefore a test, not a cited result. Genotypes may be covariates only.

Falsifying observation. The hypothesis fails if an in-range human unbound exposure that raises dihydroorotate and lowers UTP produces neither uridine-reversible myeloid differentiation of cytarabine-residual AML cells nor a selective reduction in their engraftment relative to normal CD34-positive cells. It also fails if differentiation is indifferent to uridine, or if activity is confined to oxidative-phosphorylation loss in the ROS-low fraction without differentiation of cytarabine-residual cells.

Limitations. Indication, clinical exposure, protein binding, half-life, hepatotoxicity, and teratogenicity are unverified prior knowledge and require primary-source checks. [S4] leaves approved DHODH-active drugs unproven. [S1] leaves the window of unrelated mitochondrial inhibitors unresolved. [S2] is model evidence. [S3] does not transfer to teriflunomide. Differentiation may be partial, reversible after removal, or genotype-restricted. Fatty-acid oxidation is noted in residual cells [S2]; this hypothesis does not test an inhibitor of that pathway.

Teriflunomide repurposing to drive uridine-rescuable differentiation of cytarabine-residual oxidative AML blasts

Hypothesis. In non-APL acute myeloid leukemia, teriflunomide will induce myeloid differentiation and reduce leukemogenic output of cytarabine-residual blasts that retain oxidative metabolism. The proposed mechanism is on-target dihydroorotate dehydrogenase (DHODH) inhibition with pyrimidine depletion. The intended endpoint is differentiation, kept separate from bulk cytotoxicity and from eradication of ROS-low leukemia stem cells. Teriflunomide is treated here as the active metabolite of leflunomide. Its approval for multiple sclerosis, leflunomide’s approval for rheumatoid arthritis, and assignment of DHODH as the pharmacologic target are unverified prior knowledge and require independent confirmation.

Supported premises. In the specimens studied by Lagadinou and colleagues, functionally defined leukemia stem cells frequently had low reactive oxygen species and elevated BCL-2. BCL-2 inhibition reduced oxidative phosphorylation and affected quiescent leukemia stem cells, which motivates a search for selective metabolic dependencies. That study leaves the therapeutic window of an arbitrary mitochondrial inhibitor unestablished across AML contexts [S1]. In the cytarabine models of Farge and colleagues, residual cells were not consistently enriched for immature quiescent leukemia stem cells. Those residual cells displayed oxidative-metabolism-associated mitochondrial and fatty-acid-oxidation features, and altering that state changed treatment response in the settings tested [S2]. These observations keep residual disease biologically distinct from the ROS-low stem-cell population in [S1]. DHODH inhibition promoted myeloid differentiation in experimental AML systems and affected disease-related endpoints in the models investigated, linking a metabolic enzyme to a differentiation outcome rather than to nonspecific killing alone [S4]. Venetoclax plus azacitidine is an established comparator that changes leukemia-stem-cell energy metabolism, including TCA-cycle and oxidative-phosphorylation effects, in patient-associated observations and experimental follow-up [S3]. That regimen is a mechanistic control. S4 does not establish that every approved drug affecting DHODH reproduces differentiation or achieves suitable exposure and selectivity [S4].

Speculative bridges. The packet does not identify teriflunomide or leflunomide. The first bridge is pharmacological: assumed human DHODH inhibition at exposures used for the approved indication. The second bridge joins [S4] to [S2]. DHODH is mitochondrial and donates electrons to ubiquinone (unverified prior knowledge of enzyme topology). Residual blasts with intact oxidative metabolism [S2] are therefore proposed to remain competent for DHODH-dependent pyrimidine synthesis and susceptible to its blockade, including residual populations that differ from ROS-low, BCL-2-high stem cells [S1]. The third bridge is that a uridine-rescuable maturation program will lower leukemia-initiating activity in that residual context. Genotype or mutation specificity is absent from [S1]–[S4] and is not claimed.

Alternative explanations. Marker shifts could reflect stress or selective loss of immature cells rather than a maturation program. Shared use of the ubiquinone pool could make DHODH blockade phenocopy oxidative-phosphorylation failure [S1], [S3], so energy collapse could mimic differentiation. Fatty-acid-oxidation dependence [S2] could dominate residual-cell survival and leave DHODH irrelevant. Matched normal hematopoietic progenitors could be equally sensitive. Microenvironmental pyrimidine salvage could bypass the enzyme in vivo.

Discriminating preclinical test. Compare primary non-APL AML blasts, including cytarabine-residual samples where available, after separation into ROS-low and ROS-higher fractions. Arms are teriflunomide, a tool DHODH inhibitor of the class studied in [S4], venetoclax as the BCL-2 and oxidative-phosphorylation comparator [S1], [S3], and vehicle, each with and without exogenous uridine. Score separately myeloid differentiation (morphology and maturation markers such as CD11b and CD14), bulk viability and apoptosis, oxidative phosphorylation and respiratory reserve, and leukemia-initiating or long-term culture-initiating activity. Run the same assays on matched normal CD34-positive hematopoietic cells. Confirm pathway engagement by dihydroorotate accumulation with UDP and UTP depletion. Anchor concentrations to verified human exposure for the approved indication; until those levels are checked, dose remains an assumption.

Falsifying observation. In this residual oxidative-blast context the hypothesis is disconfirmed if uridine restores pyrimidine nucleotides while differentiation and loss of leukemogenic activity persist; if teriflunomide only suppresses respiration and viability in a venetoclax-like pattern [S3] without a uridine-rescuable maturation program [S4]; if pathway engagement and phenotype appear only above verified clinical exposure; or if normal hematopoietic progenitors lose clonogenicity at the same concentrations that differentiate AML blasts.

Limitations. [S1]–[S4] do not demonstrate clinical efficacy of teriflunomide. Approval, indication, protein binding, half-life, and steady-state exposure need verification outside this packet. Cytopenias and hepatotoxicity reported for approved DHODH-inhibitor use are unverified prior knowledge and mark a marrow-selectivity risk. Nucleoside salvage, lineage bias, and genetic heterogeneity may restrict activity. This design does not set a clinical dose, a combination schedule, or a claim of superiority over existing differentiation therapy or venetoclax-based treatment.

In primary human AML that keeps a myeloid differentiation block, teriflunomide is predicted to drive functional myeloid maturation at unbound concentrations attained in its approved non-leukemia use. The mechanism under test is on-target dihydroorotate dehydrogenase (DHODH) inhibition with loss of de novo pyrimidine nucleotides. The primary endpoint is differentiation of these blasts. Survival of quiescent low-reactive-oxygen-species leukemia stem cells, and the behavior of cytarabine-residual oxidative cells, are prespecified separate endpoints.

Supported premises. DHODH inhibition promotes myeloid differentiation in experimental AML and affects disease-related endpoints in the systems studied. That evidence does not show that every approved drug affecting the pathway reproduces the result or achieves suitable exposure and selectivity [S4]. Functionally defined leukemia stem cells in the specimens studied frequently had low reactive oxygen species and elevated BCL-2. BCL-2 inhibition reduced oxidative phosphorylation and affected quiescent leukemia stem cells. This supports a defined dependency and a selectivity requirement. It does not show that an arbitrary mitochondrial inhibitor has an acceptable window across AML contexts [S1]. Residual cells after cytarabine, in the models studied, were not consistently enriched for immature quiescent leukemia stem cells. They showed mitochondrial and fatty-acid-oxidation-associated oxidative metabolism, and altering that state changed response in those settings [S2]. Venetoclax with azacitidine is an established comparator tied to leukemia-stem-cell TCA-cycle and oxidative-phosphorylation changes in patient-associated and experimental observations [S3]. Those findings remain a mechanistic benchmark. They are not transferred to teriflunomide, and repeating that regimen is not this proposal.

Unverified prior knowledge, which requires checking in primary labels before any concentration is treated as fact: teriflunomide is approved for relapsing forms of multiple sclerosis; it is the active metabolite of leflunomide, approved for rheumatoid arthritis; the class inhibits mitochondrial DHODH; protein binding, half-life, steady-state total and unbound plasma levels, hepatotoxicity, and teratogenicity lie outside [S1]-[S4]. Exogenous uridine as a pyrimidine-salvage bypass of DHODH blockade is also unverified prior knowledge, not a result from the packet.

Speculative bridges, stated as predictions: unbound teriflunomide at the verified approved exposure inhibits DHODH in AML blasts sufficiently to deplete pyrimidine nucleotides; differentiation-blocked blasts that depend on de novo pyrimidine synthesis mature, while quiescent low-ROS stem cells [S1] and cytarabine-residual oxidative cells [S2] may lack that dependence; normal CD34-positive progenitors keep clonogenicity at the same unbound level through salvage or residual enzyme capacity; maturation proceeds without the oxidative-phosphorylation collapse linked to BCL-2 inhibition [S1], [S3].

Alternative explanations. Marker gains can represent stress or incipient death. Nucleotide depletion can halt proliferation without stable lineage maturation. Confirmed off-target binding could explain the phenotype. An effect on oxidative or fatty-acid metabolism could modify residual disease [S2] while the DHODH account is incidental. Multiple-sclerosis immune actions would be absent from culture and routine xenografts. Genotype restriction could limit any single-sample result.

Discriminating preclinical test. Use primary AML that stays immature and does not mature spontaneously in short cytokine culture, paired with normal donor CD34-positive cells. After label concentrations are verified, cells see the documented unbound and total steady-state range plus one supra-therapeutic level. Panels stay separate: morphology, mature myeloid surface markers, a functional maturation assay, and colony maturity; pyrimidine nucleotides or dihydroorotate-to-orotate conversion, with exogenous uridine as the prior-knowledge DHODH bypass; oxygen consumption, ROS, and death within the low-ROS fraction, benchmarked to a BCL-2-inhibitor condition [S1], [S3]; a cytarabine-residual oxidative culture [S2]; and normal myeloid colony formation plus CD34 clonogenicity. Only uridine-sensitive AML hits advance to a patient-derived xenograft that reports marrow unbound drug, human myeloid maturation, leukemic burden, and host blood counts together.

Falsifying observation. The claim is falsified if, within verified unbound exposure for the approved indication, blasts show neither pyrimidine depletion nor functional maturation. It is falsified if uridine restores pyrimidine nucleotides and the maturation increment remains as large as in the unrescued arm. Equal loss of normal progenitor clonogenicity at that exposure falsifies selectivity. Maturation limited to the supra-therapeutic arm falsifies repurposing at clinically used exposure even when DHODH biology holds at higher concentrations.

Limitations. [S4] does not name responsive genotypes, and none is assigned here. Low-ROS quiescent cells [S1] and cytarabine-residual cells [S2] can persist after bulk differentiation. In vitro maturation can exceed clinical differentiation. Binding, residence time, hepatic injury, and teratogenicity can stop translation after a positive laboratory result. No clinical efficacy and no replacement of venetoclax plus azacitidine [S3] are claimed.

The metabolic bridge only proposes that still-respiring ROS-higher residual blasts may retain mitochondrial DHODH activity, with ubiquinone-linked topology as unverified prior knowledge, and that dihydroorotate-to-orotate flux versus uridine salvage must demonstrate it. The context bridge proposes greater uridine-rescuable loss of leukemia-initiating activity in that residual ROS-higher stratum than in ROS-low stem cells [S1] or treatment-naive bulk. Leukemia-initiating frequency and long-term culture-initiating frequency are treated as one readout, and the selectivity index divides AML loss by normal-cell loss with no floor, sample size, or variance model. Lock one initiating assay, a paired analysis with a minimum cell input for the nucleotide measurements, and a selectivity metric that remains defined when normal CD34-positive loss is near zero.

answer.answer:
Teriflunomide repurposing for uridine-rescuable differentiation of cytarabine-residual ROS-higher AML blasts

Hypothesis. In primary non-APL AML, teriflunomide at or below verified unbound Cmax will cause uridine-rescuable myeloid differentiation and lower leukemogenic output of cytarabine-residual blasts in a ROS-higher gate, only when that gate has higher baseline dihydroorotate-to-orotate flux than paired ROS-low cells. On-target DHODH inhibition is read out by reduced dihydroorotate-to-orotate flux and UDP/UTP depletion, and is scored apart from bulk kill, fatty-acid-oxidation blockade, and ROS-low stem-cell loss. Teriflunomide is treated as the active metabolite of leflunomide. Multiple-sclerosis approval, leflunomide approval for rheumatoid arthritis, and clinical DHODH targeting are unverified prior knowledge. Numeric free Cmax awaits verification.

Supported premises. Functionally defined leukemia stem cells in Lagadinou specimens frequently had low ROS and elevated BCL-2. BCL-2 inhibition reduced oxidative phosphorylation and affected quiescent leukemia stem cells, with the window for an arbitrary mitochondrial inhibitor left undefined [S1]. Farge cytarabine-residual cells were inconsistently enriched for immature quiescent leukemia stem cells, showed mitochondrial and fatty-acid-oxidation features, and changed response when that state was altered [S2]. Those residuals differ from the ROS-low population in [S1], and pyrimidine flux is unmeasured in [S2]. DHODH inhibition in Sykes models promoted myeloid differentiation and affected disease endpoints, while selectivity of each approved pathway drug stays unshown [S4]. Venetoclax with azacitidine is the established comparator for leukemia-stem-cell TCA-cycle and oxidative-phosphorylation effects [S3]. Repeating it lies outside this proposal.

Speculative bridges. The packet omits teriflunomide. Pharmacology assumes DHODH block at approved-indication unbound exposure. Oxidative and fatty-acid features [S2] stand apart from pyrimidine dependence. The proposal is that respiring ROS-higher residual blasts keep mitochondrial DHODH; ubiquinone topology is unverified prior knowledge. Stratum selectivity requires higher baseline dihydroorotate-to-orotate flux in residual ROS-higher cells than in paired ROS-low cells before any drug margin is counted, and uridine-to-UTP labeling stratifies salvage. The context claim is a larger uridine-rescuable drop in leukemia-initiating activity there than in ROS-low stem cells [S1] or treatment-naive bulk. Genotype is unspecified.

Alternative explanations. Marker gains may reflect stress or loss of immature cells. Ubiquinone sharing may collapse respiration in a venetoclax-like pattern [S1], [S3]. Fatty-acid-oxidation dependence may explain residual behavior and leave DHODH irrelevant [S2]. Normal progenitors may be equally sensitive. Marrow uridine may bypass DHODH in vivo.

Discriminating preclinical test. CellROX Deep Red, manufacturer viable-cell protocol, stains 7-AAD-negative CD45-dim blasts for 30 min at 37°C in serum-free medium, read unfixed, before any gate. Dye concordance with [S1] is unverified prior knowledge. ROS-low is the lowest quintile; ROS-higher is above the median (design choices). Cytarabine: 24 h at the sample concentration cutting bulk viability ≥70%, three washes, 48 h recovery, and continuation only if ≥2 million viable blasts remain (smaller yield = technical failure).

Stage 0, drug-free: stop unless residual ROS-higher dihydroorotate-to-orotate flux is ≥1.5× paired ROS-low flux, a design threshold. Median uridine-tracer labeling of UTP pre-declares high- and low-salvage halves. Stage 1 uses only residual ROS-higher cells, teriflunomide ≤ verified free Cmax, ± uridine at verified plasma concentration (~5 µmol/L unverified prior knowledge, replaced when checked). Go: dihydroorotate ≥2× vehicle, UDP+UTP ≤50% of vehicle, uridine restores both to within 20% of vehicle, CD11b+CD14+ rises ≥20 percentage points, and ≥30/100 blinded cells mature. n=12 primary non-APL specimens; paired Wilcoxon, two-sided α=0.05, within salvage half.

A nucleotide go precedes initiating-cell assays. Stage 2 adds strata, normal colonies, and arms ± plasma uridine: teriflunomide; brequinar matched on dihydroorotate within free Cmax (S4-class link unverified prior knowledge); venetoclax [S1], [S3]; etomoxir only if palmitate-supported OCR falls ≥50% and glucose-supported OCR stays within 20% of vehicle (CPT1 engagement unverified prior knowledge). A linear mixed model tests the treatment-by-stratum term on maturation and initiating-cell frequency with salvage half, α=0.05, in stage-0 passers only. Support is a ≥1.5× larger marker gain and initiating-cell drop in residual ROS-higher cells than in paired bulk and ROS-low cells, with CD34+ colonies ≥70% of vehicle. A xenograft of passers, unbound exposure ≤ human free Cmax, is falsified if marrow uridine holds blast UDP+UTP ≥80% of vehicle.

Falsifying observation. Falsifiers are absence of the stage-0 ≥1.5× flux excess; equal maturation by teriflunomide and brequinar in residual ROS-higher, ROS-low, and treatment-naive bulk cells [S4]; a treatment-by-stratum term under 1.5×; uridine restoration of UDP/UTP while differentiation and leukemogenic loss remain; an etomoxir or venetoclax copy without dihydroorotate accumulation and UDP/UTP depletion; concentrations above free Cmax or absent brequinar phenocopy within it; and CD34-positive colonies under 70% of vehicle. High-salvage-only misses are salvage bypass.

Limitations. [S1]–[S4] omit clinical efficacy and marrow selectivity for teriflunomide. Approval, protein binding, half-life, free Cmax, plasma uridine, brequinar potency, and etomoxir selectivity need external verification. Cytopenias and hepatotoxicity described for approved use are unverified prior knowledge and mark marrow and liver risk. n=12 is a yield lock and may underpower the interaction. Salvage, lineage bias, and genotype may restrict activity. Dose, schedule, and superiority claims are deferred.

answer.answer:
Teriflunomide repurposing to drive uridine-rescuable differentiation of cytarabine-residual oxidative AML blasts

Hypothesis. In non-APL AML, teriflunomide at or below verified unbound exposure for its approved non-AML indication will induce uridine-rescuable myeloid differentiation and lower leukemogenic output of cytarabine-residual ROS-higher blasts. The mechanism is on-target dihydroorotate dehydrogenase inhibition, read as reduced dihydroorotate-to-orotate flux and UDP/UTP depletion. Differentiation is scored apart from bulk cytotoxicity and from clearance of ROS-low leukemia stem cells. Teriflunomide is handled as the active metabolite of leflunomide. Multiple-sclerosis approval, leflunomide’s rheumatoid-arthritis approval, and DHODH as the assigned target are unverified prior knowledge. Venetoclax plus azacitidine is an established metabolic comparator [S3], and is not the repurposing claim.

Supported premises. In the Lagadinou specimens, functionally defined leukemia stem cells frequently had low reactive oxygen species and elevated BCL-2. BCL-2 inhibition reduced oxidative phosphorylation and affected quiescent leukemia stem cells, which motivates selective-dependency questions and leaves the window of an arbitrary mitochondrial inhibitor open [S1]. In the Farge cytarabine models, residual cells were not consistently enriched for immature quiescent leukemia stem cells. They displayed mitochondrial and fatty-acid-oxidation features, and altering that state changed response in the settings tested [S2]. Those data support an oxidative, FAO-associated residual state distinct from the ROS-low population in [S1]. They do not measure pyrimidine nucleotides or DHODH flux. DHODH inhibition promoted myeloid differentiation and affected disease-related endpoints in the Sykes models, connecting this enzyme to maturation rather than to nonspecific killing alone [S4]. That study does not show that every approved agent touching the pathway reproduces the result at achievable exposure [S4]. Patient-associated venetoclax–azacitidine observations link treatment to TCA-cycle and oxidative-phosphorylation changes and supply the comparator [S3].

Speculative bridges. [S1]–[S4] do not identify teriflunomide. The first bridge assumes DHODH engagement at unbound concentrations used for the approved indication. The second bridge does not treat intact respiration or FAO features [S2] as proof of de novo pyrimidine synthesis or ubiquinone availability. Mitochondrial topology of DHODH and electron transfer to ubiquinone are unverified prior knowledge. The speculation to be tested is that cytarabine-residual ROS-higher blasts maintain dihydroorotate-to-orotate flux in excess of salvage, and that this flux sustains their differentiation block, including when they differ from ROS-low, BCL-2-high stem cells [S1]. The third bridge is that uridine-rescuable maturation in this stratum reduces leukemia-initiating activity. Genotype specificity is absent from the packet and is not claimed. A further distinction from the broad [S4] effect is stratum- and exposure-restricted activity: shared DHODH blockade is predicted to meet differentiation and initiating-activity thresholds in residual ROS-higher blasts at clinical unbound exposure, and to miss those thresholds in residual ROS-low stem cells and treatment-naive bulk blasts.

Alternative explanations. Marker changes may record stress or selective loss of immature cells. Ubiquinone-pool competition may make DHODH blockade copy oxidative-phosphorylation failure [S1], [S3]. FAO dependence may dominate residual-cell survival and render DHODH irrelevant [S2]. Normal progenitors may be equally sensitive. In vivo pyrimidine salvage may bypass the enzyme. Teriflunomide may act off target in a way an engagement-matched tool inhibitor will not share.

Discriminating preclinical test. The operating rules that follow are design choices, not results from [S1]–[S4]. In primary non-APL AML, reserve a treatment-naive bulk aliquot. Expose the paired sample to cytarabine at 1 µM for 48 h, wash out for 24 h, and recover viable residual cells. Before test drug, gate residual ROS-low and ROS-higher cells as the lowest and highest quartiles of a viable-cell ROS probe. Run residual ROS-higher, residual ROS-low, and treatment-naive bulk side by side. Arms, each with and without 100 µM uridine, are vehicle, teriflunomide, an S4-class tool DHODH inhibitor adjusted to the same dihydroorotate, UDP, and UTP shift, venetoclax [S1], [S3], and a fatty-acid-oxidation inhibitor. Score morphology as the share of myelocytes and later forms, CD11b and CD14, viability and apoptosis, respiration and reserve, dihydroorotate, orotate, dihydroorotate-to-orotate conversion, uridine incorporation into UTP, UDP and UTP, and leukemia-initiating or long-term culture-initiating activity. Repeat the panel on matched normal CD34-positive cells. Teriflunomide must be tested at or below verified unbound clinical exposure; that bound is unverified prior knowledge until checked.

Success in residual ROS-higher cells requires, at that exposure, a ≥20 percentage-point increase in CD11b+CD14+ cells, a ≥15 percentage-point increase in mature myeloid forms, a ≥50% decrease in leukemia-initiating frequency, a ≥2-fold dihydroorotate rise, a ≥50% drop in UDP and UTP, and reduced dihydroorotate-to-orotate conversion with preserved salvage incorporation. Uridine must reverse each of those changes by ≥70%. The tool inhibitor must meet the same thresholds when nucleotide engagement is matched. Normal CD34-positive clonogenicity must stay ≥70% of vehicle. In the same residual fraction, the FAO-inhibitor arm falsifies DHODH relevance if it accounts for loss of viability or initiating activity while dihydroorotate-to-orotate flux and UDP/UTP remain intact and teriflunomide adds no further uridine-rescuable maturation.

Falsifying observation. The hypothesis is disconfirmed if uridine restores UDP and UTP while differentiation and loss of leukemogenic activity remain; if the pattern is venetoclax-like respiratory and viability suppression [S3] without uridine-rescuable maturation [S4]; if engagement or phenotype requires concentrations above verified unbound exposure; or if normal CD34-positive clonogenicity falls below 70% of vehicle. It fails when only the broad [S4] effect is present, defined as residual ROS-low stem cells and treatment-naive bulk meeting the same marker, morphology, and initiating-activity thresholds. It fails if every DHODH blocker produces that same cross-stratum pattern, and if teriflunomide’s residual ROS-higher phenotype is absent from the tool inhibitor after dihydroorotate, UDP, and UTP are matched.

Limitations. [S1]–[S4] do not demonstrate clinical efficacy, protein binding, half-life, or unbound exposure of teriflunomide. Cytopenias and hepatotoxicity associated with approved DHODH-inhibitor use are unverified prior knowledge and flag marrow selectivity. The cytarabine pulse, ROS quartiles, uridine concentration, and numeric cutoffs are analysis choices, not a clinical dose or schedule. Nucleoside salvage, lineage bias, and genetic heterogeneity may limit activity. The study does not claim superiority over differentiation therapy or venetoclax-based treatment.

Initiating-cell frequency and the xenograft falsifier are not operational assays, and “brequinar matched on dihydroorotate within free Cmax” does not state a matching rule. Specify limiting-dilution leukemia-initiating frequency in the same specimens, dose-match brequinar to teriflunomide’s dihydroorotate AUC at verified unbound Cmax, and name xenograft strain, n, schedule, and unbound exposure confirmation.

Selectivity rests on an n=12 treatment-by-stratum test further split by salvage half, a brequinar arm matched to an undefined free Cmax for an unapproved comparator, and an unnamed leukemia-initiating-cell assay. critique: The target stratum is operationalized as the highest ROS quartile, while S2 only supports cytarabine-residual cells with mitochondrial and fatty-acid-oxidation features that are not consistently leukemia-stem-cell enriched, and S1 ROS-low stem cells are themselves oxidative-phosphorylation dependent. Requiring the same differentiation and initiating-activity thresholds to fail in treatment-naive bulk blasts is an added restriction that S4's broader differentiation result does not motivate and that no salvage-versus-de-novo measurement explains. Recast the naive-bulk arm as a quantitative comparator and add a pyrimidine-flux assay that would account for any residual-selective effect.

The tool DHODH inhibitor and the fatty-acid-oxidation inhibitor are unnamed, and one primary sample cannot supply ROS-quartile splits, ten drug–uridine arms, and leukemia-initiating readouts after a 1 µM cytarabine pulse. Name both comparators, make unbound clinical exposure versus DHODH engagement an explicit go/no-go, and stage the study so uridine-rescuable morphology plus nucleotide engagement is primary, with initiating activity and normal CD34 clonogenicity run only after that gate.

ROS gating therefore misses the S2 population and treats residual ROS-low cells as stem cells. Select on mitochondrial mass, oxygen-consumption rate, or fatty-acid-oxidation dependence, and record ROS only as a covariate.

The dose ceiling is an empty unbound-exposure placeholder, and both the engagement-matched DHODH tool inhibitor and the fatty-acid-oxidation inhibitor are unnamed, so the discriminating arms cannot be executed. Name those two comparators and lock teriflunomide to a cited unbound Css or Cmax before any phenotype is scored.

Success is an AND of uncalibrated cutoffs across surface markers, morphology, initiating-cell frequency, and several metabolites, while leukemia-initiating and long-term culture-initiating assays are left interchangeable. Pre-specify one primary endpoint—uridine-reversible loss of initiating activity together with on-target UDP/UTP depletion inside the exposure cap—and move the percentage-point cutoffs to secondary analyses with a single chosen initiating-cell assay.
